items.stem: Which expression is equivalent to NOT(A.B) by De Morgan's law?
options: A + B
A.B
A̅ + B̅
A̅.B̅
items.answer: A̅ + B̅
items.markingKey: Break the bar and change the operator: NOT(A.B) = A̅ + B̅.

items.stem: Explain why simplifying a Boolean expression is useful when designing a circuit.
items.answer: A simpler expression needs fewer gates, so the circuit is cheaper, uses less power, produces less heat and is faster.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point, max 2 [2]

items.stem: Explain how De Morgan's laws allow a circuit to be built using only NAND gates.
items.answer: De Morgan's laws convert ORs into NAND form (A + B = NOT(A̅.B̅)), so any sum-of-products can be written as NANDs of NANDs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Which expression is equivalent to NOT(A.P)?
options: A̅ + P̅
NOT(A + P)
items.answer: A̅ + P̅
items.markingKey: De Morgan's law.

items.stem: Simplify the Boolean expression NOT(Y̅ + Q̅), stating the law(s) used.
items.answer: Y.Q
items.markingKey: De Morgan's law then double negation (1); answer Y.Q (1) [2]

items.stem: Simplify the Boolean expression X.R + X.R̅, stating the law(s) used.
items.answer: X

items.stem: Freya claims that the expression C.B + C.B.Y can be replaced by C.B in a circuit for Pioneer Insurance. (a) Use Boolean algebra to show whether this is correct. (b) Verify your answer with a truth table for the inputs B, C, Y. (c) State how many gates are saved, counting each AND, OR and NOT as one gate.
items.answer: (a) Correct: absorption: A.B(1 + C) = A.B (b) both expressions give the same output in every row (c) 4 − 1 = 3 gates saved
items.markingKey: (a) law applied [2] (b) table with all rows [2] (c) 3 [1]

items.stem: Tariq claims that the expression P + P.X can be replaced by P in a circuit for Lakeside College. (a) Use Boolean algebra to show whether this is correct. (b) Verify your answer with a truth table for the inputs P, X. (c) State how many gates are saved, counting each AND, OR and NOT as one gate.
items.answer: (a) Correct: absorption: A + A.B = A(1 + B) = A (b) both expressions give the same output in every row (c) 2 − 0 = 2 gates saved
items.markingKey: (a) law applied [2] (b) table with all rows [2] (c) 2 [1]

items.stem: What is A + 1 equal to?
options: A
A̅
items.markingKey: Null (annulment) law for OR.

items.stem: What is A.A̅ equal to?
options: A̅
A
items.markingKey: Complement law: A AND NOT A is always 0.

items.stem: Priya applies De Morgan's law and writes NOT(B + X) = B̅ + X̅. Explain the error and give the correct result.
items.answer: When the bar is broken the operator must also change (OR to AND): NOT(B + X) = B̅.X̅.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: operator must change; 1 mark: correct expression [2]

items.stem: Priya applies De Morgan's law and writes NOT(Q.Y) = Q̅.Y̅. Explain the error and give the correct result.
items.answer: When the bar is broken the operator must also change (AND to OR): NOT(Q.Y) = Q̅ + Y̅.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: operator must change; 1 mark: correct expression [2]

items.stem: Assertion (A): A + A.B simplifies to A. Reason (R): A + A.B = A(1 + B) and 1 + B = 1. Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
items.markingKey: A is true and R gives the reason for it.

items.stem: Which expression is equivalent to A + A?
options: A + A.1
A̅
A
items.answer: A
items.markingKey: idempotent law.

items.stem: Simplify the Boolean expression B + C + A + B as far as possible, showing your working.
items.answer: A + B + C
items.markingKey: Truth table outputs 01111111; laws such as absorption, distribution and complement give A + B + C. 1 mark per correct simplification step, 1 mark final answer [3]

items.stem: Simplify the Boolean expression P.C + P.C̅, stating the law(s) used.
items.answer: P

items.answer: (a) Correct: absorption: A.(A + B) = A (b) both expressions give the same output in every row (c) 2 − 0 = 2 gates saved
items.markingKey: (a) law applied [2] (b) table with all rows [2] (c) 2 [1]

items.stem: In a Karnaugh map, why are the rows and columns labelled in Gray code order (00, 01, 11, 10)?
options: So that adjacent cells differ by only one variable
Because binary order is not allowed
To make the map symmetrical
To reduce the number of cells
items.answer: So that adjacent cells differ by only one variable
items.markingKey: This allows neighbouring 1s to be grouped and a variable eliminated.

items.stem: Explain why groups in a K-map should be as large as possible.
items.answer: Each larger group eliminates more variables, giving shorter product terms and a simpler expression.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain why a cell may be included in more than one group.
items.answer: Overlapping lets each group be as large as possible, which simplifies the expression; every 1 must be covered at least once.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A logic function of A, B, C has the truth table (ABC→X): 000→0, 001→1, 010→1, 011→0, 100→1, 101→1, 110→0, 111→0. Use a Karnaugh map to find the simplified sum-of-products expression.
items.answer: X = A̅.B.C̅ + A.B̅ + B̅.C
items.markingKey: K-map filled correctly (1); groups: A̅.B.C̅; A.B̅; B̅.C (1); X = A̅.B.C̅ + A.B̅ + B̅.C (1) [3]

items.stem: A logic function of A, B, C has the truth table (ABC→X): 000→0, 001→1, 010→1, 011→0, 100→0, 101→0, 110→1, 111→0. Use a Karnaugh map to find the simplified sum-of-products expression.
items.answer: X = A̅.B̅.C + B.C̅
items.markingKey: K-map filled correctly (1); groups: A̅.B̅.C; B.C̅ (1); X = A̅.B̅.C + B.C̅ (1) [3]

items.stem: A logic function of A, B, C, D has the truth table (ABCD→X): 0000→0, 0001→0, 0010→0, 0011→0, 0100→0, 0101→1, 0110→1, 0111→0, 1000→0, 1001→1, 1010→0, 1011→1, 1100→1, 1101→1, 1110→1, 1111→1. Use a Karnaugh map to find the simplified sum-of-products expression.
items.answer: X = A.B + A.D + B.C̅.D + B.C.D̅
items.markingKey: K-map filled correctly (1); groups: A.B; A.D; B.C̅.D; B.C.D̅ (2); X = A.B + A.D + B.C̅.D + B.C.D̅ (1) [4]

items.answer: (a) 11110111 (b) X = A̅.B̅.C̅ + A̅.B̅.C + A̅.B.C̅ + A̅.B.C + A.B̅.C + A.B.C̅ + A.B.C (c) X = A̅ + B + C (d) 0 AND, 2 OR, 1 NOT
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) [1] (c) correct groups [2]; X = A̅ + B + C [1] (d) [1]

items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) [1] (c) correct groups [2]; X = A + C + D [1] (d) [1]

items.stem: Which group sizes are allowed in a Karnaugh map?
options: Any number of cells
Only pairs
Multiples of 3
items.markingKey: Groups must be rectangles of 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 cells.

items.stem: A group of four 1s in a 3-variable K-map eliminates how many variables?
items.markingKey: A group of 2ⁿ cells eliminates n variables.

items.stem: Assertion (A): A group of four 1s removes two variables. Reason (R): The two variables that change within the group cancel out. Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

items.markingKey: A is true and R gives the reason for it.

A is true but R is false

items.stem: Which gates make a half adder?
options: A NAND and a NOR gate
An AND gate for the sum and an XOR gate for the carry
An XOR gate for the sum and an AND gate for the carry
Two OR gates
items.answer: An XOR gate for the sum and an AND gate for the carry
items.markingKey: S = A XOR B; C = A AND B.

items.stem: Explain how full adders can be combined to add two 4-bit numbers.
items.answer: Four full adders are connected in series; the carry-out of each is the carry-in of the next more significant bit (ripple carry adder).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain why a flip-flop is described as bistable.
items.answer: It has two stable states (Q = 0 or Q = 1) and stays in one until an input changes it, so it stores a bit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A half adder has inputs A = 0 and B = 0. State the sum S and carry C, and the gates that produce them.
items.answer: S = 0, C = 0; XOR for S, AND for C

items.stem: A 4-bit ripple carry adder made from full adders adds 1010 and 0011. Give the 4-bit sum, the final carry-out, and the carry-out of each full adder from the least significant bit.
items.answer: Sum 1101; carry-out 0; carries (LSB first) 0100
items.markingKey: sum (1); final carry (1); carry chain (1) [3]

items.stem: Riverside Medical Centre is designing an arithmetic unit and a register for a simple processor. (a) Draw (describe) a half adder and give its truth table. (b) Explain why flip-flops are used to build registers.
items.answer: (a) XOR gate gives S, AND gate gives C; truth table AB 00→S0 C0, 01→1 0, 10→1 0, 11→0 1. (b) Each flip-flop stores one bit; n flip-flops clocked together store an n-bit value.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark gates; 1 mark truth table [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: How many inputs does a full adder have?
items.markingKey: A, B and carry-in; outputs sum and carry-out.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Flip-flops are used in registers. Reason (R): It must add the carry from the previous, less significant bit. Which option is correct?

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

items.stem: Ines is designing a 4-bit adder for a teaching kit developed in Madrid. (a) Explain why a half adder cannot be used for every bit of a multi-bit adder. (b) Explain why the SR flip-flop input S = 1, R = 1 must be avoided.
items.answer: (a) It has no carry-in input, so it cannot add the carry from the previous bit; full adders are needed. (b) Both outputs are forced to the same value, so Q and Q̅ are not complements; the next state is unpredictable.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: An SR flip-flop (built from NOR gates) receives the inputs (S, R): (0, 1), (0, 0), (0, 0), (1, 0) in order. Give the value of Q after each input, writing "unchanged" where the input holds the previous state.
items.markingKey: S = 1 sets Q to 1, R = 1 resets Q to 0, S = R = 0 holds: 0, 0, 0, 1 [2]

items.stem: Mohammed applies De Morgan's law and writes NOT(X.Y) = X̅.Y̅. Explain the error and give the correct result.
items.answer: When the bar is broken the operator must also change (AND to OR): NOT(X.Y) = X̅ + Y̅.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: operator must change; 1 mark: correct expression [2]

options: R + (R + B)
R̅
R
items.answer: R

options: R
items.answer: R

items.answer: B̅

items.stem: Ravi claims that the expression P.B + P.B.A can be replaced by P.B in a circuit for Pioneer Insurance. (a) Use Boolean algebra to show whether this is correct. (b) Verify your answer with a truth table for the inputs A, B, P. (c) State how many gates are saved, counting each AND, OR and NOT as one gate.
items.answer: (a) Correct: absorption: A.B(1 + C) = A.B (b) both expressions give the same output in every row (c) 4 − 1 = 3 gates saved
items.markingKey: (a) law applied [2] (b) table with all rows [2] (c) 3 [1]

items.stem: Kwame claims that the expression (B + Q).(B + Q̅) can be replaced by B in a circuit for Horizon Travel. (a) Use Boolean algebra to show whether this is correct. (b) Verify your answer with a truth table for the inputs B, Q. (c) State how many gates are saved, counting each AND, OR and NOT as one gate.
items.answer: (a) Correct: A + B.B̅ = A + 0 = A (b) both expressions give the same output in every row (c) 4 − 0 = 4 gates saved
items.markingKey: (a) law applied [2] (b) table with all rows [2] (c) 4 [1]

items.stem: Can a K-map group wrap around the edges of the map?
options: Only diagonally
Yes, the edges are adjacent
No, never
Only for 2-variable maps
items.answer: Yes, the edges are adjacent
items.markingKey: The map is treated as wrapping left-right and top-bottom.

items.stem: Assertion (A): K-map groups can contain three cells. Reason (R): The two variables that change within the group cancel out. Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
items.answer: A is false but R is true
items.markingKey: A is false: "K-map groups can contain three cells." is incorrect; R is a true statement.

items.stem: Assertion (A): A Karnaugh map uses Gray code ordering. Reason (R): Cells on opposite edges differ in only one variable. Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
items.answer: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
items.markingKey: A and R are both true statements, but R does not explain A.

items.stem: Write the sum-of-products expression for the truth table (ABC→X): 000→1, 001→1, 010→0, 011→0, 100→0, 101→1, 110→1, 111→1.
items.answer: X = A̅.B̅.C̅ + A̅.B̅.C + A.B̅.C + A.B.C̅ + A.B.C
items.markingKey: one minterm per row with X = 1 [3]

items.answer: X = A̅.B̅.C̅ + A.B̅.C̅ + A.B.C

items.stem: Write the sum-of-products expression for the truth table (ABC→X): 000→1, 001→1, 010→0, 011→1, 100→0, 101→0, 110→1, 111→0.

items.stem: A control circuit at Starlight Cinemas has output X = A NAND ((NOT (B OR D) NAND A) OR C). (a) Complete the truth table for ABCD = 0…0 to 1…1. (b) Write the sum-of-products expression. (c) Use a Karnaugh map to simplify the expression. (d) State the number of 2-input AND/OR gates and NOT gates needed for your simplified expression.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) [1] (c) correct groups [2]; X = A̅ + B̅.C̅.D̅ [1] (d) [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In an SR flip-flop built from NOR gates, which input combination is invalid? (b) Why is the JK flip-flop an improvement on the SR flip-flop?
items.answer: (a) S = 1, R = 1 (b) It has no invalid input state and is clocked
items.markingKey: (a) Both outputs would be forced to 0, so Q and Q̅ are not complementary. (b) J = K = 1 toggles instead of being invalid; the clock synchronises changes.

items.stem: A memory circuit at FreshFarm Foods is built from flip-flops. Explain the purpose of the clock input of a JK flip-flop.
items.answer: Synchronises changes so the output only changes on a clock pulse, keeping circuits in step.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Amara is designing a 4-bit adder for a teaching kit developed in Karachi. (a) Explain why the SR flip-flop input S = 1, R = 1 must be avoided. (b) Explain the purpose of the clock input of a JK flip-flop.
items.answer: (a) Both outputs are forced to the same value, so Q and Q̅ are not complements; the next state is unpredictable. (b) Synchronises changes so the output only changes on a clock pulse, keeping circuits in step.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A half adder has inputs A = 0 and B = 1. State the sum S and carry C, and the gates that produce them.
items.answer: S = 1, C = 0; XOR for S, AND for C

items.stem: Omar is building digital circuits for a student project at SkyLink Airways. (a) Draw (describe) a half adder and give its truth table. (b) Explain why flip-flops are used to build registers.
items.answer: (a) XOR gate gives S, AND gate gives C; truth table AB 00→S0 C0, 01→1 0, 10→1 0, 11→0 1. (b) Each flip-flop stores one bit; n flip-flops clocked together store an n-bit value.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark gates; 1 mark truth table [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]
